data.name: NewProjectHelpNameTitle
data.value: Your product's name

data.name: NewProjectHelpNameLead
data.value: It names your project's folder and its code, so it uses English letters and numbers and starts with a letter: Bluebird, AcmeCrm or Contoso.Shop. The name your users see is separate: it can be anything, in any language, and you can change it any time.

data.name: NewProjectHelpNameAdvice
data.value: Use the name you'd use today. It's easy to change.

data.name: NewProjectHelpNameLater
data.value: Rename the app to Bluebird Plus

data.name: NewProjectFaqRename
data.value: Can I rename my project later?

data.name: NewProjectFaqRenameAnswer
data.value: Yes. Ask your AI to rename it. The folders and the code are renamed together.

data.name: NewProjectFaqEnglishLetters
data.value: Why only English letters?

data.name: NewProjectFaqEnglishLettersAnswer
data.value: The name becomes part of your code, where only English letters and numbers work everywhere. The name people see in the app, the stores and the browser tab can be in any language.

data.name: NewProjectFaqKeepName
data.value: Do you keep the name?

data.name: NewProjectFaqKeepNameAnswer
data.value: No. bitfabric.co keeps nothing about your project: not its name, your choices, your code, your data or your prompts.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGoalTitle
data.value: A real product, or a quick try?

data.name: NewProjectHelpGoalLead
data.value: A real product is set up the way it will run for your customers, with a full database (PostgreSQL) that runs on your computer while you build. A quick try skips that: your data sits in one file, and a few sample pages show how a screen, its data and the server fit together.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGoalAdvice
data.value: Building something you want to launch? Pick real product. Only curious? A quick try is ready sooner and installs less.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGoalLater
data.value: Make this project ready for production: move it to PostgreSQL and remove the sample pages

data.name: NewProjectDemoSamplePages
data.value: See the sample pages live

data.name: NewProjectFaqTryToReal
data.value: Can a quick try become my real product?

data.name: NewProjectFaqTryToRealAnswer
data.value: Yes, it's the same project. Ask your AI to move it to PostgreSQL and remove the sample pages.

data.name: NewProjectFaqRealInstallsMore
data.value: Why does a real product install more?

data.name: NewProjectFaqRealInstallsMoreAnswer
data.value: Its database runs on your computer in a container, so the setup adds a free container engine to run it. It's the same database your server runs once you publish, so nothing changes then.

data.name: NewProjectFaqGoalCost
data.value: Does either one cost anything?

data.name: NewProjectFaqGoalCostAnswer
data.value: No. Both use free tools on your computer. What costs money comes later: the AI you build with, and the server you publish to.

data.name: NewProjectHelpStartTitle
data.value: What it starts with

data.name: NewProjectHelpStartLead
data.value: Every project already has sign-up and sign-in with passkeys and two-step verification, profiles, roles and permissions, settings, 12 languages, and light and dark themes. On top of that, it can start with an admin panel or an online store.

data.name: NewProjectHelpStartAdvice
data.value: Building a tool businesses use? Start with the admin panel and turn its products into your own things. Selling products? Start with the store.

data.name: NewProjectHelpStartLater
data.value: Add the admin panel with its dashboard

data.name: NewProjectDemoAdminPanel
data.value: See the admin panel live

data.name: NewProjectDemoStore
data.value: See the store live

data.name: NewProjectFaqAdminPanel
data.value: What's in the admin panel?

data.name: NewProjectFaqAdminPanelAnswer
data.value: A dashboard with charts, and pages to manage products and categories with search, sorting and paging. With the assistant and live updates on, the dashboard changes the moment the data does.

data.name: NewProjectFaqStore
data.value: What's in the online store?

data.name: NewProjectStartStoreText
data.value: A shop front with products and their pages, ready to make your own.

data.name: NewProjectFaqBoth
data.value: Can I have both?

data.name: NewProjectFaqBothAnswer
data.value: Not in one go today. Start with the one closest to your product and ask your AI to build the rest.

data.name: NewProjectFaqCodeMine
data.value: Is the code mine to change?

data.name: NewProjectFaqCodeMineAnswer
data.value: All of it. Whatever you start with is your own code, in your free GitHub account.

data.name: NewProjectHelpCustomersLead
data.value: With multi-tenancy, one app serves many companies. Each company has its own users and sees only its own data, and one person can belong to several companies. Most software sold to businesses (SaaS) works this way.

data.name: NewProjectHelpCustomersAdvice
data.value: Selling to businesses? Keep several customer companies. Building for one organization, like your own company? Pick one organization.

data.name: NewProjectHelpCustomersLater
data.value: Add multi-tenancy, so each customer company sees only its own data

data.name: NewProjectDemoTenants
data.value: Try it in the admin panel demo

data.name: NewProjectFaqTryDemo
data.value: How do I try it in the demo?

data.name: NewProjectFaqTryDemoAnswer
data.value: Sign in to the admin panel demo as store-user@bitplatform.dev with the password 12345678, and switch between the companies that user belongs to.

data.name: NewProjectFaqDataApart
data.value: How is each company's data kept apart?

data.name: NewProjectFaqDataApartAnswer
data.value: On the server: the app only reads and writes the data of the company the user is signed in to, and nothing in the browser can change that.

data.name: NewProjectFaqCustomersLater
data.value: Can I change this later?

data.name: NewProjectFaqCustomersLaterAnswer
data.value: Yes, either way, by asking your AI. If you think you'll sell to businesses, starting with it is simpler.

data.name: NewProjectHelpFeaturesTitle
data.value: The AI assistant and notifications

data.name: NewProjectHelpFeaturesLead
data.value: The AI assistant lives inside your app and answers your users' questions, and can look things up in your app's data. It comes with live updates: open screens change the moment the data does. Push notifications reach your users on their phones, computers and browsers.

data.name: NewProjectHelpFeaturesAdvice
data.value: Keep both unless you're sure you won't need them. Taking something out later is easier than adding it.

data.name: NewProjectHelpFeaturesLater
data.value: Add the AI assistant to the app

data.name: NewProjectFaqAssistantCost
data.value: Does the AI assistant cost anything?

data.name: NewProjectFaqAssistantCostAnswer
data.value: It needs a key from an AI provider such as OpenAI, which charges by use. Until you add a key, the assistant stays hidden.

data.name: NewProjectFaqAssistantNotBuilder
data.value: Is it the AI I build my app with?

data.name: NewProjectFaqAssistantNotBuilderAnswer
data.value: No. It's an assistant for the people who use your app. You build the app with an AI agent of your own, such as Claude Code, which opens with your project at the end.

data.name: NewProjectFaqPushCost
data.value: Do push notifications cost anything?

data.name: NewProjectFaqPushCostAnswer
data.value: No. Your server sends them straight to Apple, Google and the browsers, with no paid service in between.

data.name: NewProjectHelpErrorsTitle
data.value: Errors and logs

data.name: NewProjectHelpErrorsLead
data.value: Every app meets errors sometimes: a payment that fails, a page that doesn't load. Your app writes down each one with what led to it, so you and your AI can find the cause and fix it. This decides where it writes them.

data.name: NewProjectHelpErrorsAdvice
data.value: Not sure? Keep them on your own server, without additional cost and with no other account. Pick Sentry if you want your Android and iOS apps' crashes caught too, or the service your team already uses.

data.name: NewProjectHelpErrorsLater
data.value: Send the app's errors to Sentry

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsCost
data.value: What does each one cost?

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsCostAnswer
data.value: On your own server, nothing more than the server you already pay for. Sentry is free for one person and up to 5,000 errors a month, and its team plan starts at about $26 a month. Application Insights charges for what it keeps: the first 5 GB a month are free, then about $2.30 for each GB. Their prices change, so check sentry.io and azure.microsoft.com before you pay.

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsAccount
data.value: Do I need an account for Sentry or Application Insights?

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsAccountAnswer
data.value: Yes, in your own name: Sentry's at sentry.io, or an Azure account for Application Insights. Your project is ready for it, and your AI walks you through pasting its key.

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsSeen
data.value: Does bit Fabric see my errors?

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsSeenAnswer
data.value: No. They stay on your server or go to your own account at Sentry or Microsoft. bit Fabric only sees your app's health: whether it and each of its parts are up.

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsLater
data.value: Can I change it later?

data.name: NewProjectFaqErrorsLaterAnswer
data.value: Yes. Ask your AI to send them somewhere else, and it adds what that needs.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDevicesTitle
data.value: Where you try it today

data.name: NewProjectHelpDevicesLead
data.value: Every project has all five apps: web, Android, iPhone and iPad, Windows and Mac. This only decides which ones get set up on this computer now. Each native app adds a few GB of tools and some minutes to the setup.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDevicesAdvice
data.value: In a hurry? Keep only the web. You can still open your app on your phone, in its browser, through a link your project gives you.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDevicesLater
data.value: Set up the Android app on this computer

data.name: NewProjectFaqPhone
data.value: Can I see it on my phone without these?

data.name: NewProjectFaqPhoneAnswer
data.value: Yes. While your app runs, the project gives you a secure link and a QR code. Scan it with your phone, use the app in its browser, and add it to your home screen if you like.

data.name: NewProjectFaqLoseApps
data.value: Do I lose the mobile apps if I pick only the web?

data.name: NewProjectFaqLoseAppsAnswer
data.value: No. The code of all five apps is always in your project. This only sets up the tools to build them on this computer.

data.name: NewProjectFaqIphoneOnWindows
data.value: Can I build the iPhone app on Windows?

data.name: NewProjectFaqIphoneOnWindowsAnswer
data.value: Not on Windows itself: Apple's tools only run on a Mac. Your project still has the iPhone app, ready for when you have one.

data.name: NewProjectFaqAndroidNeeds
data.value: What does Android need?

data.name: NewProjectFaqAndroidNeedsAnswer
data.value: About 8 GB of downloads, and 16 GB of memory for the phone emulator. You can also plug in your own Android phone instead.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDatabaseTitle
data.value: Where your data lives

data.name: NewProjectHelpDatabaseLead
data.value: PostgreSQL is free, popular and the safe choice for a real product. SQLite keeps everything in one file and installs nothing, which suits a quick try. SQL Server and MySQL are there if your company or your host already uses them.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDatabaseAdvice
data.value: Not sure? Keep PostgreSQL.

data.name: NewProjectHelpDatabaseLater
data.value: Move the database from SQLite to PostgreSQL

data.name: NewProjectFaqInstallDatabase
data.value: Do I have to install a database?

data.name: NewProjectFaqInstallDatabaseAnswer
data.value: No. The setup runs it for you in a container while you build, and your server runs it once you publish.

data.name: NewProjectFaqSqlServer
data.value: Anything to know about SQL Server?

data.name: NewProjectFaqSqlServerAnswer
data.value: On a Linux server only SQL Server Express is free, with up to 50 GB for each database and no scheduled backups.

data.name: NewProjectFaqMySql
data.value: Anything to know about MySQL?

data.name: NewProjectMySqlLicense
data.value: Your project reaches MySQL through Oracle's library, which is under the GPL: an app whose code you keep closed needs a commercial license from Oracle.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGitHubTitle
data.value: A private GitHub repository

data.name: NewProjectHelpGitHubLead
data.value: GitHub keeps your code and its whole history safe in your own account, and later checks every change and publishes your app to your server. The setup creates a private repository and puts your code in it; you sign in to GitHub once, in your browser.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGitHubAdvice
data.value: Keep it on. A free GitHub account is enough, and you can make one when the setup asks you to sign in.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGitHubLater
data.value: Create a private GitHub repository for this project and push it

data.name: NewProjectFaqWhoSeesCode
data.value: Who can see my code?

data.name: NewProjectFaqWhoSeesCodeAnswer
data.value: Only you and the people you invite. The repository is private, and it's in your account, not ours.

data.name: NewProjectFaqGitLab
data.value: My team uses GitLab. What should I do?

data.name: NewProjectFaqGitLabAnswer
data.value: Turn this off and push the project yourself. Your AI can turn the project's GitHub workflows into GitLab pipelines.

data.name: NewProjectHelpOfflineTitle
data.value: Working without internet

data.name: NewProjectHelpOfflineLead
data.value: Your app normally reads and saves its data on your server, so it needs internet. With this, it also keeps a copy of its data on each phone, computer and browser: people go on working offline, and what they change is sent to your server once they're back online.

data.name: NewProjectHelpOfflineAdvice
data.value: Keep it off unless people really must work without internet, like in a warehouse or out in the field. It makes the web app a few MB bigger and slower to start.

data.name: NewProjectHelpOfflineLater
data.value: Add the offline database

data.name: NewProjectDemoOffline
data.value: See an offline app live

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineSync
data.value: How does the app catch up with the server?

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineSyncAnswer
data.value: It keeps a small database on the device, in the browser too. What people change offline is sent to your server once they're back online. The sample to-do list shows how; your own data needs the same setup, which your AI can do.

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineSize
data.value: How much heavier does it make the web app?

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineSizeAnswer
data.value: About 2 MB more for the web app to download, and a slower first start.

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineLater
data.value: Can I add it later?

data.name: NewProjectFaqOfflineLaterAnswer
data.value: Yes. Ask your AI to add the offline database.

data.name: NewProjectHelpLineTitle
data.value: About the line you paste

data.name: NewProjectHelpLineLead
data.value: It runs bit Fabric's installer, which sets up the tools your project needs, then creates your project with the answers you gave. Everything happens on your computer, step by step, and every step says what it's doing.

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineSafe
data.value: Is it safe to paste a line from a website?

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineSafeAnswer
data.value: Only from bitfabric.co. Scammers copy pages like this one and change the line, so check that the address bar says bitfabric.co before you copy. The installer is signed, and you can read it before you run it.

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineChanges
data.value: Will it change my computer?

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineChangesAnswer
data.value: It adds the tools your project needs, each only if it's missing, and you can remove them like any other app. It changes nothing else.

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineAdmin
data.value: Do I need an administrator password?

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineAdminAnswer
data.value: Mostly not, as the tools install for your user. Windows may ask once to allow a change, such as turning on what the database container needs. Choose Yes.

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineFails
data.value: What if something fails?

data.name: NewProjectFaqLineFailsAnswer
data.value: The other steps carry on. At the end you see what failed, with the exact line that fixes it. If you're stuck, write to us.

data.name: NewProjectHelpGeneralTitle
data.value: Before you start

data.name: NewProjectFaqCode
data.value: Do I need to know how to code?

data.name: NewProjectFaqCodeAnswer
data.value: No. You tell your AI what you want in plain words; it builds it, runs the tests and explains the change. You paste one line, once.

data.name: NewProjectFaqAccount
data.value: Do I need an account?

data.name: NewProjectFaqAccountAnswer
data.value: No. You make one later only if you want us to watch your live app and tell you when something breaks.

data.name: NewProjectFaqCost
data.value: What does it cost?

data.name: NewProjectFaqCostAnswer
data.value: Creating your project costs nothing. Building and running it does: an AI agent such as Claude Pro (about $20 a month), a server once you publish (about €5 a month), and the app stores if you publish there (Apple $99 a year, Google $25 once).

data.name: NewProjectFaqReady
data.value: Is it ready for real customers?

data.name: NewProjectFaqReadyAnswer
data.value: Yes. Sign-in with passkeys and two-step verification, roles and permissions, each company's data kept apart on the server, and automatic tests and checks are there from the first minute.

data.name: NewProjectFaqWhatWeSee
data.value: What do you see of my project?

data.name: NewProjectFaqWhatWeSeeAnswer
data.value: Its name and the choices you make here, so we can help if something goes wrong. Never your code, your data or your prompts.

data.name: NewProjectFaqDisappears
data.value: What if bit Fabric disappears?

data.name: NewProjectFaqDisappearsAnswer
data.value: Your app keeps working. Its code is in your free GitHub account and its data on your server; nothing of it runs on ours.

data.name: NewProjectFaqComputer
data.value: Which computer do I need?

data.name: NewProjectFaqComputerAnswer
data.value: Windows 10 or 11, a Mac, or Linux, with at least 8 GB of memory (16 GB for Android) and about 20 GB of free space.

data.name: NewProjectFaqOnPhone
data.value: Can I do this on my phone?

data.name: NewProjectFaqOnPhoneAnswer
data.value: You can answer the questions here and send them to your computer. The project itself is created on a computer.

data.value: This name can't name a project: use English letters and numbers, with no spaces, starting with a letter. The name people see in the app can still be in any language: ask your AI to change it once your project is open.

data.name: ScanFindingHttpsRedirectMissing
data.value: Your app's http:// address doesn't send visitors to https://

data.name: ScanFindingHttpsRedirectMissingWhy
data.value: Someone who types your address without https:// gets a page anyone on their network can read and change.

data.name: ScanFindingHttpsRedirectMissingFix
data.value: Redirect every http:// request to https:// with a 301 or 308: keep app.UseHttpsRedirection() in Server.Web and the api, or turn on Always Use HTTPS in Cloudflare.

data.name: ScanFindingHstsMissing
data.value: Browsers aren't told to always use HTTPS for your app (no HSTS)

data.name: ScanFindingHstsMissingWhy
data.value: Without Strict-Transport-Security, a visitor's first request can still go over plain http, where it can be intercepted.

data.name: ScanFindingHstsMissingFix
data.value: Send Strict-Transport-Security: max-age=31536000; includeSubDomains on every https response: app.UseHsts() outside Development, or the HSTS setting of your CDN.

data.name: ScanFindingHstsShort
data.value: HTTPS is enforced for only {0} days (HSTS max-age)

data.name: ScanFindingHstsShortWhy
data.value: A short max-age lets a browser forget it within days, so a later visit may start over plain http again. Six months is the least that counts.

data.name: ScanFindingHstsShortFix
data.value: Raise max-age to at least 15768000 (six months), better 31536000 (a year), in your HSTS options or your CDN.

data.name: ScanFindingCspMissing
data.value: No Content-Security-Policy is set

data.name: ScanFindingCspMissingWhy
data.value: Without one, a script someone manages to inject into a page runs with your users' sign-in and data.

data.name: ScanFindingCspMissingFix
data.value: Send a Content-Security-Policy header from Server.Web, starting from default-src 'self'; script-src 'self' 'wasm-unsafe-eval'; frame-ancestors 'self', then allow only the other origins your app really uses.

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeInline
data.value: Your Content-Security-Policy still lets inline scripts run ('unsafe-inline')

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeInlineWhy
data.value: 'unsafe-inline' in script-src lets an injected script run anyway, which is most of what the policy is for.

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeInlineFix
data.value: Remove 'unsafe-inline' from script-src and default-src. Move inline scripts into files, or allow each one by a nonce or a hash.

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeEval
data.value: Your Content-Security-Policy lets scripts run text as code ('unsafe-eval')

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeEvalWhy
data.value: eval() turns data into code, a common way an injected value becomes an attack. Blazor WebAssembly needs only 'wasm-unsafe-eval'.

data.name: ScanFindingCspUnsafeEvalFix
data.value: Replace 'unsafe-eval' with 'wasm-unsafe-eval' in script-src, or remove it when no library of yours calls eval().

data.name: ScanFindingFrameProtectionMissing
data.value: Other sites can show your app inside a frame

data.name: ScanFindingFrameProtectionMissingWhy
data.value: A page that frames yours can trick your users into clicking buttons they can't see (clickjacking).

data.name: ScanFindingFrameProtectionMissingFix
data.value: Add frame-ancestors 'self' to your Content-Security-Policy, or send X-Frame-Options: SAMEORIGIN.

data.name: ScanFindingNosniffMissing
data.value: Browsers may guess the type of your files (no X-Content-Type-Options)

data.name: ScanFindingNosniffMissingWhy
data.value: A browser that guesses may run an uploaded file as a script.

data.name: ScanFindingNosniffMissingFix
data.value: Send X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff on every response, from Server.Web and the api.

data.name: ScanFindingReferrerPolicyMissing
data.value: No Referrer-Policy is set

data.name: ScanFindingReferrerPolicyMissingWhy
data.value: Without one, older browsers send the full address of a page, its query string included, to every site it links to.

data.name: ScanFindingReferrerPolicyMissingFix
data.value: Send Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin from Server.Web.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotSecure
data.value: Cookies go over plain http too: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotSecureWhy
data.value: A cookie without Secure travels unencrypted whenever the browser makes an http request, where anyone on the network can read it.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotSecureFix
data.value: Set Secure on these cookies: CookieSecurePolicy.Always in the cookie's options, or Secure = true where the app appends it.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotHttpOnly
data.value: Scripts can read sign-in cookies: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotHttpOnlyWhy
data.value: A session cookie that JavaScript can read is stolen by the first script someone injects.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNotHttpOnlyFix
data.value: Set HttpOnly on these cookies (HttpOnly = true in their options), unless the app's own scripts really need to read them.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNoSameSite
data.value: Cookies don't say which sites may send them: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNoSameSiteWhy
data.value: Without SameSite, older browsers attach them to requests other sites start, which cross-site request forgery relies on.

data.name: ScanFindingCookieNoSameSiteFix
data.value: Set SameSite=Lax, or Strict, in these cookies' options.

data.name: ScanFindingServerVersionDisclosed
data.value: Your server says which software and version it runs: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingServerVersionDisclosedWhy
data.value: A version number tells an attacker which known flaws to try first.

data.name: ScanFindingServerVersionDisclosedFix
data.value: Remove these headers: AddServerHeader = false in Kestrel's options, and X-Powered-By and X-AspNet-Version in your reverse proxy or hosting settings.

data.name: ScanFindingHealthzOpen
data.value: Your app's detailed health report is open to everyone

data.name: ScanFindingHealthzOpenWhy
data.value: /healthz lists every service your app depends on with its errors, which can carry host names and database queries.

data.name: ScanFindingHealthzOpenFix
data.value: Keep /healthz behind its authorization, as the template maps it: MapAppHealthChecks with AppFeatures.System.Operations_View. Leave only /health and /alive anonymous.

data.name: ScanFindingHangfireOpen
data.value: The background jobs dashboard (/hangfire) is open to everyone

data.name: ScanFindingHangfireOpenWhy
data.value: Anyone can see, rerun and delete your app's background jobs, and read their arguments.

data.name: ScanFindingHangfireOpenFix
data.value: Keep HangfireDashboardAuthorizationFilter in UseHangfireDashboard's options in Server.Api, and don't replace it with a filter that lets everyone in.

data.name: ScanFindingDevMcpOpen
data.value: dev-mcp answers without asking anyone to sign in

data.name: ScanFindingDevMcpOpenWhy
data.value: /dev-mcp lets an AI read your live app's data, logs and background jobs. Open, it hands them to anyone.

data.name: ScanFindingDevMcpOpenFix
data.value: Map /dev-mcp with RequireAuthorization(OAuthEndpoints.AuthorizationFor(OAuthResources.DevMcpPath)) in Server.Api, as the template does.

data.name: ScanFindingApiDocsOpen
data.value: Your API's docs are open to everyone

data.name: ScanFindingApiDocsOpenWhy
data.value: The docs map every endpoint of your api with its parameters, which makes the next step of an attack easy.

data.name: ScanFindingApiDocsOpenFix
data.value: Map OpenAPI and Scalar only outside Production, as the template does in Server.Api (if (app.Environment.IsProduction() is false)), or put them behind sign-in.

data.name: ScanFindingODataMetadataOpen
data.value: Your OData data model ($metadata) is open to everyone

data.name: ScanFindingODataMetadataOpenWhy
data.value: $metadata describes every entity your api serves and how they relate: a map of your data.

data.name: ScanFindingODataMetadataOpenFix
data.value: Require sign-in on the route that serves /odata, or don't add the route components that publish $metadata.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpired
data.value: The TLS certificate of {0} has expired

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpiredWhy
data.value: Browsers refuse to open the app and show a security warning instead.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpiredFix
data.value: Renew the certificate now, then find out why it didn't renew itself: your host's or Cloudflare's automatic renewal, or the certbot timer.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpiresSoon
data.value: The TLS certificate of {0} expires in {1} days

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpiresSoonWhy
data.value: Once it expires, browsers refuse to open the app. From February 2027 certificates last at most 64 days, so renewing them has to be automatic.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateExpiresSoonFix
data.value: Check that automatic renewal works (your host, Cloudflare or certbot), and renew the certificate now if it hasn't.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateNameMismatch
data.value: The TLS certificate of {0} is for another name

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateNameMismatchWhy
data.value: Browsers show a security warning instead of your app.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateNameMismatchFix
data.value: Issue a certificate that names {0}, or a wildcard that covers it, and install it on the server or the CDN that answers there.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateChainInvalid
data.value: Browsers can't trust the TLS certificate of {0}

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateChainInvalidWhy
data.value: It is self-signed, from an unknown authority, or misses its intermediate certificate, so some browsers and apps refuse to connect.

data.name: ScanFindingCertificateChainInvalidFix
data.value: Install a certificate from a public authority such as Let's Encrypt, with its full chain (fullchain.pem rather than cert.pem).

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpired
data.value: The registration of {0} has ended

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpiredWhy
data.value: Once the registrar's grace period is over, the domain stops working and anyone can register it.

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpiredFix
data.value: Renew it at your registrar today, and turn on automatic renewal.

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpiresSoon
data.value: The registration of {0} ends in {1} days

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpiresSoonWhy
data.value: When it ends, your app, its emails and its sign-in links stop working.

data.name: ScanFindingDomainExpiresSoonFix
data.value: Renew it at your registrar, and turn on automatic renewal with a payment method that won't expire.

data.name: ScanFindingNoIndex
data.value: Search engines are told not to list these pages (noindex)

data.name: ScanFindingNoIndexWhy
data.value: A page with noindex never shows up in Google, however good it is.

data.name: ScanFindingNoIndexFix
data.value: Remove noindex from the robots meta tag and the X-Robots-Tag header of public pages; keep it only on pages that need sign-in.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsBlocksAll
data.value: robots.txt tells every search engine to stay away

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsBlocksAllWhy
data.value: Disallow: / for every user agent keeps your whole app out of search results.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsBlocksAllFix
data.value: In robots.txt, replace Disallow: / with the paths that really must stay out, such as /api/ and the pages that need sign-in.

data.name: ScanFindingNotPrerendered
data.value: These pages reach search engines empty, without their text

data.name: ScanFindingNotPrerenderedWhy
data.value: The HTML your server sends has almost no text, so search engines and link previews see an empty app shell until scripts run.

data.name: ScanFindingNotPrerenderedFix
data.value: Turn prerendering on for public pages (PrerenderEnabled in Server.Web's appsettings.json), and keep pages that only work in a browser out of the sitemap.

data.name: ScanFindingTitleMissing
data.value: These pages have no title

data.name: ScanFindingTitleMissingWhy
data.value: The title is the line search results show as the link; without one, search engines make one up.

data.name: ScanFindingTitleMissingFix
data.value: Give each of these pages a title of 30 to 60 characters that says what it is about: PageTitle of AppPageData in a bit app.

data.name: ScanFindingTitleLength
data.value: These pages' titles are too short or too long

data.name: ScanFindingTitleLengthWhy
data.value: Search results cut titles at about 60 characters, and a very short one says too little to be clicked.

data.name: ScanFindingTitleLengthFix
data.value: Rewrite each title to 30 to 60 characters, the main words first.

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionMissing
data.value: These pages have no description

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionMissingWhy
data.value: Search results show the description under the title; without one, they show whatever text they pick from the page.

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionMissingFix
data.value: Give each of these pages a meta description of 70 to 160 characters: Description of AppPageData in a bit app.

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionLength
data.value: These pages' descriptions are too short or too long

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionLengthWhy
data.value: Search results cut descriptions at about 160 characters, and a very short one leaves the space to text they pick themselves.

data.name: ScanFindingDescriptionLengthFix
data.value: Rewrite each description to 70 to 160 characters that make someone want to open the page.

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateTitles
data.value: These pages share one title: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateTitlesWhy
data.value: Search engines can't tell same-titled pages apart, and may show only one of them.

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateTitlesFix
data.value: Give each of these pages a title of its own that says what sets it apart.

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateDescriptions
data.value: These pages share one description

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateDescriptionsWhy
data.value: A description repeated across pages tells search engines nothing about any of them.

data.name: ScanFindingDuplicateDescriptionsFix
data.value: Write a description of its own for each of these pages.

data.name: ScanFindingCanonicalMissing
data.value: These pages don't name their canonical address

data.name: ScanFindingCanonicalMissingWhy
data.value: A page reached by several addresses, with and without a culture or a query string, splits its ranking between them.

data.name: ScanFindingCanonicalMissingFix
data.value: Add <link rel="canonical" href="..."> with the page's preferred address to the head of each page.

data.name: ScanFindingLangMissing
data.value: These pages don't say which language they are in

data.name: ScanFindingLangMissingWhy
data.value: Without <html lang>, search engines and screen readers may read the page in the wrong language.

data.name: ScanFindingLangMissingFix
data.value: Set lang on the html element to the page's culture, such as <html lang="en-US">.

data.name: ScanFindingHreflangMissing
data.value: These pages don't point to their other languages (hreflang)

data.name: ScanFindingHreflangMissingWhy
data.value: Without hreflang, search engines may show a page in the wrong language to people searching in another.

data.name: ScanFindingHreflangMissingFix
data.value: Add <link rel="alternate" hreflang="..." href="..."> for each culture the page exists in, and one with hreflang="x-default".

data.name: ScanFindingSocialPreviewMissing
data.value: Links to these pages show no preview when shared ({0} missing)

data.name: ScanFindingSocialPreviewMissingWhy
data.value: Without og:title and og:image, a link shared on WhatsApp, LinkedIn or X shows as a bare address.

data.name: ScanFindingSocialPreviewMissingFix
data.value: Add <meta property="og:title"> and <meta property="og:image">, with an image of 1200×630, to each public page.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutAlt
data.value: {0} images have no text alternative

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutAltWhy
data.value: Screen readers and search engines can't tell what an image without alt shows.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutAltFix
data.value: Give each image an alt text that says what it shows, or alt="" for a purely decorative one; on BitImage, its Alt parameter.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtMissing
data.value: Your app has no robots.txt

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtMissingWhy
data.value: robots.txt tells search engines what to skip, such as /api/, and where your sitemap is.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtMissingFix
data.value: Serve /robots.txt with User-agent: *, the paths to skip and a Sitemap: line with your sitemap's full address, as UseSiteMap in Server.Web does.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtNoSitemap
data.value: robots.txt doesn't say where your sitemap is

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtNoSitemapWhy
data.value: Search engines find new pages sooner through a sitemap they are told about.

data.name: ScanFindingRobotsTxtNoSitemapFix
data.value: Add a Sitemap: line with your sitemap's full address to robots.txt; the template adds it in Production.

data.name: ScanFindingSitemapMissing
data.value: Your app has no sitemap

data.name: ScanFindingSitemapMissingWhy
data.value: A sitemap lists your public pages, so search engines find all of them, not only those linked from the home page.

data.name: ScanFindingSitemapMissingFix
data.value: Serve /sitemap.xml with every public page in every culture, as UseSiteMap in Server.Web does.

data.name: ScanFindingLcpSlow
data.value: The main content takes {0} s to show on a phone

data.name: ScanFindingLcpSlowWhy
data.value: Largest Contentful Paint (LCP) is when the biggest text or image of the page shows. Google counts over 2.5 s as needing improvement and over 4 s as poor, and visitors leave a page that stays blank.

data.name: ScanFindingLcpSlowFix
data.value: Keep prerendering on for public pages and cache them with [AppResponseCache] so the CDN answers them, serve the main image small and early (not loading="lazy"), and keep scripts and styles from holding up the first paint.

data.name: ScanFindingClsHigh
data.value: The page moves as it loads, a layout shift of {0} on a phone

data.name: ScanFindingClsHighWhy
data.value: Cumulative Layout Shift (CLS) measures how much content jumps while the page loads, which makes people tap the wrong thing. Google counts over 0.1 as needing improvement and over 0.25 as poor.

data.name: ScanFindingClsHighFix
data.value: Give images, videos and embeds a width and height or an aspect-ratio, reserve the space of what loads later, such as ads and banners, and don't insert content above what is already shown.

data.name: ScanFindingTbtHigh
data.value: The page doesn't respond for {0} ms while it loads on a phone

data.name: ScanFindingTbtHighWhy
data.value: Total Blocking Time (TBT) adds up the time scripts keep the page from answering a tap or a key while it loads; it stands in for INP, which needs a real visitor. Over 200 ms needs improvement and over 600 ms is poor.

data.name: ScanFindingTbtHighFix
data.value: Do less in scripts while the page loads: prerender public pages so they show before WebAssembly starts, move heavy work out of the first render (OnAfterFirstRenderAsync), lazy-load assemblies only some pages use (BlazorWebAssemblyLazyLoad), and load third-party scripts later.

data.name: ScanFindingFcpSlow
data.value: Nothing shows for {0} s on a phone

data.name: ScanFindingFcpSlowWhy
data.value: First Contentful Paint (FCP) is when the first text or image shows. Google counts over 1.8 s as needing improvement and over 3 s as poor; until then the visitor looks at a blank screen.

data.name: ScanFindingFcpSlowFix
data.value: Keep prerendering on and cache public pages with [AppResponseCache], cut the CSS and fonts the first view waits for, and link to the page itself rather than through a redirect, such as http to https or / to the culture's path.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesTooBig
data.value: Images could be {0} KiB smaller

data.name: ScanFindingImagesTooBigWhy
data.value: Images bigger than they're shown, or in older formats, take longest to download on a phone's connection and delay the page's main content.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesTooBigFix
data.value: Serve images in WebP or AVIF, at the size they're shown, with srcset and sizes for smaller screens, and compress them; start with the files listed.

data.name: ScanFindingFilesNotCached
data.value: Files downloaded again on every visit: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingFilesNotCachedWhy
data.value: Without a long cache lifetime, a returning visitor's browser downloads the same scripts, styles and images again, so every visit is as slow as the first.

data.name: ScanFindingFilesNotCachedFix
data.value: Send Cache-Control: public, max-age=31536000, immutable for files whose name or query carries a version, as the template's fingerprinted _framework and _content files do, give the others a version too, and cache public pages at the CDN with [AppResponseCache(SharedMaxAge = ...)].

data.name: ScanFindingRenderBlocking
data.value: Scripts and styles hold up the first view by {0} ms

data.name: ScanFindingRenderBlockingWhy
data.value: The browser draws nothing until it has downloaded and run the CSS and scripts in the head, so each one on that path delays what the visitor sees.

data.name: ScanFindingRenderBlockingFix
data.value: Load scripts with defer or at the end of the body, as blazor.web.js already is in a template app, inline or preload the little CSS the first view needs, and load the rest without blocking.

data.name: ScanFindingUnusedCode
data.value: Scripts and styles could be {0} KiB smaller

data.name: ScanFindingUnusedCodeWhy
data.value: Code the page downloads but doesn't use, duplicated or not minified, still comes over the network and is parsed, which slows the first view on a phone the most.

data.name: ScanFindingUnusedCodeFix
data.value: Publish in Release so files are trimmed and minified, drop libraries the pages don't use, lazy-load assemblies only some pages need (BlazorWebAssemblyLazyLoad with LazyAssemblyLoader), and keep each page's styles in its scoped .razor.scss file.

data.name: ScanFindingMainThreadBusy
data.value: The browser spends {0} s running the page's code

data.name: ScanFindingMainThreadBusyWhy
data.value: While scripts run and the page is styled and laid out, the browser can't answer the visitor, and a phone does this several times slower than a computer.

data.name: ScanFindingMainThreadBusyFix
data.value: Prerender public pages so they show before scripts start, move heavy work out of the first render (OnAfterFirstRenderAsync), avoid reading the layout right after changing it, and lazy-load what the first view doesn't need; the files listed take the most time.

data.name: ScanFindingThirdPartyCode
data.value: Third parties that slow the page down: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingThirdPartyCodeWhy
data.value: Chat widgets, analytics, ads and embeds from other sites download and run on every page, and the page waits for them.

data.name: ScanFindingThirdPartyCodeFix
data.value: Drop the third parties you don't need, and load the rest after the page shows, on interaction, or with async or defer.

data.name: ScanFindingPageSlowToArrive
data.value: The page takes {0} ms to start arriving

data.name: ScanFindingPageSlowToArriveWhy
data.value: Everything else waits for the page's HTML: a slow answer from the server, a redirect on the way or a page sent uncompressed delays the whole load.

data.name: ScanFindingPageSlowToArriveFix
data.value: Cache public pages with [AppResponseCache] so the CDN answers them (ResponseCaching:EnableCdnEdgeCaching in Server.Web's appsettings.json), keep the server near your users, compress responses, and link to the final address rather than through a redirect.

data.name: ScanFindingLcpImageFoundLate
data.value: The page's main image is found late

data.name: ScanFindingLcpImageFoundLateWhy
data.value: When the largest image is lazy-loaded, set by a script or named only in CSS, the browser finds it after everything else and the main content shows late.

data.name: ScanFindingLcpImageFoundLateFix
data.value: Put the main image in the HTML as an img with fetchpriority="high" and without loading="lazy", or preload it with <link rel="preload" as="image">.

data.name: ScanFindingLayoutShiftCauses
data.value: Elements that move the page as it loads: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingLayoutShiftCausesWhy
data.value: Images without a size, fonts that swap and content inserted late push away what the visitor is reading or about to tap.

data.name: ScanFindingLayoutShiftCausesFix
data.value: Give images and embeds a width and height or an aspect-ratio, reserve space for late content, and animate with transform and opacity rather than size and position.

data.name: ScanFindingFontsHideText
data.value: Text stays invisible while web fonts load

data.name: ScanFindingFontsHideTextWhy
data.value: A web font without font-display hides the text until it arrives, which on a phone's connection can take seconds.

data.name: ScanFindingFontsHideTextFix
data.value: Add font-display: swap (or optional) to every @font-face, and preload the one font the first view uses.

data.name: ScanFindingDomTooLarge
data.value: The page has {0} elements

data.name: ScanFindingDomTooLargeWhy
data.value: A very large page takes long to style, lay out and update, and every change to it costs more, above all on a phone.

data.name: ScanFindingDomTooLargeFix
data.value: Render long lists and grids virtualized (BitBasicList or BitDataGrid with Virtualize), page the rest, and keep hidden parts such as closed menus and tabs out of the page until they open.

data.name: ScanFindingOldHttpProtocol
data.value: Requests still made over HTTP/1.1: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingOldHttpProtocolWhy
data.value: HTTP/1.1 needs a connection for every few files, while HTTP/2 and HTTP/3 carry them all over one, which matters most on a phone's slower network.

data.name: ScanFindingOldHttpProtocolFix
data.value: Turn HTTP/2 or HTTP/3 on where the app is served: at the CDN or the reverse proxy (Cloudflare has them on by default), or in Kestrel, which speaks HTTP/2 over TLS.

data.name: ScanFindingPageTooHeavy
data.value: The page downloads {0} KiB

data.name: ScanFindingPageTooHeavyWhy
data.value: Every KiB costs time on a phone's connection, and money on a metered plan.

data.name: ScanFindingPageTooHeavyFix
data.value: Compress and resize images, drop unused libraries, publish in Release, and lazy-load what the first view doesn't need.

data.name: ScanFindingBackForwardCacheBlocked
data.value: Going back loads the page again instead of showing it at once

data.name: ScanFindingBackForwardCacheBlockedWhy
data.value: Browsers keep a page in their back-forward cache to show it instantly when the visitor goes back, unless something on the page stops them.

data.name: ScanFindingBackForwardCacheBlockedFix
data.value: Avoid unload handlers and Cache-Control: no-store on pages, and close open connections such as WebSockets when the page is hidden (pagehide), then open them again on pageshow.

data.name: ScanFindingViewportNotSet
data.value: The page isn't set up for phone screens

data.name: ScanFindingViewportNotSetWhy
data.value: Without a viewport meta tag, a phone draws the page at a computer's width, shrinks it, and waits before every tap.

data.name: ScanFindingViewportNotSetFix
data.value: Add <meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1"> to the head, as App.razor does in a template app.

data.name: ScanFindingPerformanceAuditFailed
data.value: Lighthouse's {0} check fails

data.name: ScanFindingPerformanceAuditFailedWhy
data.value: Lighthouse found something that slows these pages down, which bit Fabric has no words of its own for yet.

data.name: ScanFindingPerformanceAuditFailedFix
data.value: Open these pages in Chrome, run Lighthouse from DevTools, and do what its {0} check lists.

data.name: ScanFindingContrastTooLow
data.value: Text that's hard to read against its background: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingContrastTooLowWhy
data.value: Text whose color is too close to its background's, such as light grey prices, is hard to read for people with low vision and for anyone in bright sunlight. WCAG asks for a contrast of 4.5:1, or 3:1 for large text.

data.name: ScanFindingContrastTooLowFix
data.value: Use the theme's foreground colors (BitColor and BitCss.Class.Color.Foreground) instead of light greys, or darken the text until it reaches 4.5:1, in light and dark mode alike; a link inside text also needs an underline, not its color alone.

data.name: ScanFindingButtonsWithoutName
data.value: Buttons with no name for screen readers: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingButtonsWithoutNameWhy
data.value: A screen reader announces such a button as just "button", so someone who can't see it doesn't know what it does.

data.name: ScanFindingButtonsWithoutNameFix
data.value: Give each icon-only button an AriaLabel (BitButton's AriaLabel parameter), or visible text that says what it does.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutDescription
data.value: Images with no text alternative for screen readers: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutDescriptionWhy
data.value: Someone using a screen reader hears nothing, or the file's name, for an image without alt, and misses what it shows.

data.name: ScanFindingImagesWithoutDescriptionFix
data.value: Give each meaningful image an alt text that says what it shows, and a purely decorative one alt=""; on BitImage, its Alt parameter.

data.name: ScanFindingLinksWithoutName
data.value: Links with no name for screen readers: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingLinksWithoutNameWhy
data.value: A link that is only an icon, or an image without alt, is announced as just "link", so someone who can't see it doesn't know where it goes.

data.name: ScanFindingLinksWithoutNameFix
data.value: Give each link text that says where it goes, or an AriaLabel when it is only an icon.

data.name: ScanFindingFieldsWithoutLabel
data.value: Form fields with no label: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingFieldsWithoutLabelWhy
data.value: Without a label, a screen reader can't say what a field is for, and a placeholder is gone as soon as someone types.

data.name: ScanFindingFieldsWithoutLabelFix
data.value: Give every field one label: BitTextField's Label, or an AriaLabel where no label shows.

data.name: ScanFindingPageLanguageWrong
data.value: The page doesn't say its language correctly

data.name: ScanFindingPageLanguageWrongWhy
data.value: A screen reader reads a page in the language its html element names, so a missing or wrong lang makes Persian or English sound garbled.

data.name: ScanFindingPageLanguageWrongFix
data.value: Set lang on the html element to the page's culture, such as <html lang="en-US"> or <html lang="fa-IR">, and lang on any part in another language.

data.name: ScanFindingZoomBlocked
data.value: The page doesn't let people zoom in

data.name: ScanFindingZoomBlockedWhy
data.value: user-scalable=no, or a maximum-scale below 5, stops people with low vision from enlarging the text on their phone.

data.name: ScanFindingZoomBlockedFix
data.value: Remove user-scalable=no and maximum-scale from the viewport meta tag: width=device-width, initial-scale=1 is enough.

data.name: ScanFindingAriaMisused
data.value: Elements whose ARIA roles or attributes don't fit them: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingAriaMisusedWhy
data.value: Wrong ARIA tells a screen reader something an element isn't, such as a menu without items, or a hidden part that can still get the focus, which is worse than no ARIA at all.

data.name: ScanFindingAriaMisusedFix
data.value: Prefer the native element, or the Bit.BlazorUI component that already has the right roles, and use only the ARIA roles and attributes that are valid where they are, with the children and parents they require.

data.name: ScanFindingTapTargetsTooSmall
data.value: Buttons and links too small or too close together to tap: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingTapTargetsTooSmallWhy
data.value: Targets under 24 by 24 pixels, or packed together, are hard to hit with a finger, above all for people whose hands shake.

data.name: ScanFindingTapTargetsTooSmallFix
data.value: Make buttons and links at least 24 by 24 CSS pixels with space between them, for example with the theme's control sizes ($bit-size-control-md).

data.name: ScanFindingStructureUnclear
data.value: Headings, lists or tables that don't say how the page is built: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingStructureUnclearWhy
data.value: Screen reader users move through a page by its headings, lists, tables and landmarks; skipped heading levels, fake lists and tables without headers leave them lost.

data.name: ScanFindingStructureUnclearFix
data.value: Use headings in order (one h1, then h2, h3...), real ul, ol and li for lists, th for table headers, and one main landmark a page; on BitText, its Element parameter sets the heading level.

data.name: ScanFindingKeyboardNavigation
data.value: Parts of the page that are hard to use with a keyboard: {0}

data.name: ScanFindingKeyboardNavigationWhy
data.value: People who can't use a mouse move with Tab: a tabindex above 0 jumbles that order, and without a way to skip the menu they tab through it on every page.

data.name: ScanFindingKeyboardNavigationFix
data.value: Don't use a tabindex above 0, add a skip link to the main content, give frames a title, and keep access keys unique.

data.name: ScanFindingAccessibilityAuditFailed
data.value: Lighthouse's {0} accessibility check fails

data.name: ScanFindingAccessibilityAuditFailedWhy
data.value: Lighthouse found something on these pages that keeps some people from using them, which bit Fabric has no words of its own for yet.

data.name: ScanFindingAccessibilityAuditFailedFix
data.value: Open these pages in Chrome, run Lighthouse from DevTools, and do what its {0} check lists.

data.name: AboutBitFabricPageTitle
data.value: About bit Fabric: what the name means, and who makes it

data.name: AboutBitFabricPageDescription
data.value: What the name bit Fabric means, the principles it's built on, and who makes it: BitPlatform, in the Netherlands, the team behind bit platform.

data.name: AboutEyebrow
data.value: About bit Fabric

data.name: AboutTitle
data.value: The warp is ready. You weave the weft.

data.name: AboutLead
data.value: bit Fabric gives you the warp: an app that's full featured on day one, on web, Android, iOS, Windows and macOS. Your own AI weaves your product into it on your computer, and it runs on your own server. That's what the name means.

data.name: AboutStoryTitle
data.value: What the name means

data.name: AboutStoryIntro
data.value: On a loom, the warp is the set of threads held tight before weaving starts, and the weft is the thread woven through them, which makes the pattern. A fabric needs both.

data.name: AboutWarpTitle
data.value: The warp: ready on day one

data.name: AboutWarpText
data.value: What every app needs, built and tested before your first prompt: a complete identity solution, many companies in one app, an admin panel, an AI assistant, any language, and apps for every device.

data.name: AboutWeftTitle
data.value: The weft: your idea

data.name: AboutWeftText
data.value: The pages, the rules and the look that make your product yours. Your AI weaves them in on your computer, and spends its time on what only you can describe.

data.name: AboutFabricTitle
data.value: The fabric: all yours

data.name: AboutFabricText
data.value: One piece, and every thread of it yours: the code in your repository, the app on your server, your users in your own database. Nothing of it is with us.

data.name: AboutPrinciplesTitle
data.value: The principles it's built on

data.name: AboutPrinciplesIntro
data.value: When two ways of building something pull in different directions, these decide.

data.name: AboutPrincipleYoursTitle
data.value: Yours from the start

data.name: AboutPrincipleYoursText
data.value: Your code, repository, database, server and keys are made in your own accounts. There's no Export button, because nothing of yours is with us.

data.name: AboutPrincipleProductFirstTitle
data.value: What you get comes first

data.name: AboutPrincipleProductFirstText
data.value: Every page shows what you get before how to get it. The one line you paste comes last, with plain words on where to paste it.

data.name: AboutPrincipleQuietTitle
data.value: One line, then quiet

data.name: AboutPrincipleQuietText
data.value: The line you paste asks you nothing and shows each step as it goes. If a step fails, it says what failed and the exact line that fixes it.

data.name: AboutPrincipleExplainTitle
data.value: Explained before it happens

data.name: AboutPrincipleExplainText
data.value: Before anything is installed, you see what it is, how big it is and how long it takes. Before a large change, your AI tells you its plan.

data.name: AboutPrincipleWordsTitle
data.value: Your words, not jargon

data.name: AboutPrincipleWordsText
data.value: You're asked about your business, not about technology. Where a technical term helps, it comes in brackets, as in: an app for several customer companies (multi-tenancy).

data.name: AboutPrincipleReadOnlyTitle
data.value: Your live app is read-only to AI

data.name: AboutPrincipleReadOnlyText
data.value: Your AI can read your live app's data and logs to find a problem, but can't change them. Anything that would let an AI change your live app has to ask you first, every time.

data.name: AboutPrincipleCostTitle
data.value: The cost before the spending

data.name: AboutPrincipleCostText
data.value: Your AI plan, your server, the app stores' accounts and the cost of each SMS are written out before you commit to any of them.

data.name: AboutPrincipleSafeTitle
data.value: Safe from the first version

data.name: AboutPrincipleSafeText
data.value: What a project starts with has to be safe for real users: sign-in checked on the server, encrypted connections and limits on repeated attempts. Security must never depend on asking your AI the right way.

data.name: AboutPrincipleReplaceableTitle
data.value: Everything of ours can be replaced

data.name: AboutPrincipleReplaceableText
data.value: Monitoring reads a standard health report that any other monitor can read too, and your status page and its history can be exported. If you leave bit Fabric, your app doesn't even notice.

data.value: Besides your agent, the line installs the tools your project needs, into your user folder, with no administrator rights.

data.name: CompareQuestionWhichAi
data.value: Which AI can I use?

data.name: CompareAnswerWhichAi
data.value: The agent you already use: Copilot, Codex, Claude, Gemini, Antigravity or Cursor, or a model on your own computer, which keeps everything there. The project carries its own instructions and skills, so it works the same whichever you pick. Since 18 June 2026, Gemini CLI no longer serves personal Google accounts, and Google points them to Antigravity.

data.name: CompareQuestionAfterBeta
data.value: What happens when the beta ends?

data.name: CompareAnswerAfterBeta
data.value: That isn't decided yet. Whatever it becomes will be published on the pricing page before it applies. Either way, the app you built stays yours and keeps working.

data.name: CompareQuestionHosting
data.value: Does bit Fabric host my app?

data.name: CompareAnswerHosting
data.value: No, by design. Your app runs on a Linux server you choose, rented or your own, so nothing of it is with us. Your AI sets up its deployment through GitHub.

data.name: CompareQuestionReplaceAgent
data.value: Does bit Fabric replace my AI agent?

data.name: CompareAnswerReplaceAgent
data.value: No. bit Fabric is what your agent starts from. Your agent still does the building, on your computer, guided by the project's own instructions and skills.

data.name: CompareQuestionChangeAnything
data.value: Can I still change anything?

data.name: CompareAnswerChangeAnything
data.value: Yes. Every line is yours, in your own repository, and your AI changes any part of it the way it would on an empty project.

data.name: CompareQuestionTokens
data.value: Doesn't it use more tokens than an empty project?

data.name: CompareAnswerTokens
data.value: On a single task it can look that way, because your AI does more before it builds: it plans with you, writes what you decided into the project for your team and every later session, tries the screens in every state of their data, reviews the work and adds tests. Across a real product, that is exactly what saves: far less back-and-forth and rework, mistakes caught before they cost you, and security and performance thought about from day one. So the project as a whole costs less. Many people build with bit Fabric on Claude's $20 plan.

data.name: CompareQuestionCheaper
data.value: Isn't a hosted builder cheaper?

data.name: CompareAnswerCheaper
data.value: For a landing page or a small, simple app, yes: one plan covers it. For a serious product, one whose future matters to you, bit Fabric costs far less. Your AI plan comes straight from its maker, and a plan goes much further than the same money spent on credits. Your server comes straight from a host, from about €4 a month, with nobody's share on top. Your tests run on the computer you already have, so they cost nothing extra, and every bill comes from whoever does the work.

data.name: CompareQuestionIsKit
data.value: Is bit Fabric a starter kit?

data.name: CompareAnswerIsKit
data.value: No. bit Fabric doesn't sell code. Your project is made on your computer and in your own accounts, and what comes with it is the way from an idea to a live app: design, an AI that works like a team, deployment, upgrades and monitoring.

data.name: CompareQuestionNewVersions
data.value: How do new versions reach a project I've changed?

data.name: CompareAnswerNewVersions
data.value: Your AI brings each new version in with the template-diff skill, keeping the changes you made, and runs the tests before it says it's done.

data.name: CompareQuestionWhichOne
data.value: Which one should I choose?

data.name: CompareAnswerWhichOne
data.value: If you want your app and its data run for you, a hosted builder. If you want to choose every part and build the foundations yourself, your AI on an empty project. If you want code to build on, a starter kit. If you want all of it in your own accounts and full featured on five platforms from day one, bit Fabric.

data.name: CompareLovableTitle
data.value: bit Fabric and Lovable, side by side

data.name: CompareLovableAnswer
data.value: Lovable is the better choice if you want a web app built and run for you on Lovable's cloud, with the code synced to Git even on its free plan. bit Fabric is the better choice if you want your app on every device and in your own accounts, built by your own AI.

data.name: CompareLovableCard
data.value: Where your app, its data and its keys live, and what pauses when credits run out

data.name: CompareLovableDoesWell
data.value: Two-way Git sync on every plan, the free one included; its export carries your users and their password hashes; a Europe region for your app's data

data.name: CompareLovableDayOne
data.value: A web app built from your prompts, with a database, users' accounts, file storage and server functions run by Lovable

data.name: CompareLovableWhere
data.value: Lovable Cloud runs your app's database, your users' accounts and your keys, in a region you pick once; or you connect your own Supabase

data.name: CompareLovableStopPaying
data.value: At zero credits, building stops, the AI in your app fails, and your app's database, files and users' accounts pause: the data can't be reached or exported until they run again. Published pages keep serving

data.name: CompareLovablePlatforms
data.value: Web. Its own apps for iOS, Android and the desktop are for building; publishing yours to the stores wasn't found in its documentation

data.name: CompareLovableCost
data.value: A free plan with 5 credits a day. Pro from $25 a month for 100 credits, up to $2,250 for 10,000; the same credits pay for building, hosting, your app's database and the AI in your app

data.name: CompareLovableAi
data.value: Lovable's own agent, paid in credits per message, so your prompts go to Lovable; the AI in your app runs through Lovable's AI gateway

data.name: CompareLovableGoingLive
data.value: Publishing is built in. Hosting is free for most small or new apps, heavier traffic is paid in credits, and custom domains start on Pro

data.name: CompareLovableLeaving
data.value: The code goes with Git sync, and your users with their password hashes. Your app's database moves by hand, and only to Supabase; the keys stored in Lovable, its AI gateway calls and its connections to other services don't move

data.name: CompareLovableSourceLine
data.value: Every fact about Lovable comes from its own documentation and pricing, read on {0}. Each number leads to its source.

data.name: CompareLovableMoveQuestion
data.value: Can I move my Lovable app to bit Fabric?

data.name: CompareLovableMoveAnswer
data.value: Yes, by rebuilding it rather than importing it. Your Lovable app's code is in your Git repository, so your AI can read it, rebuild its features on bit Fabric with the port skill, and then help bring your data over.

data.name: ForCopilotDescription
data.value: GitHub Copilot on a bit Fabric project: it reads AGENTS.md and the project's skills on its own in VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs and the terminal, and takes a model of your choice with your own key.

data.name: ForCopilotLead
data.value: It reads the project's instructions and skills on its own, so your requests go to your idea.

data.name: ForCopilotCard
data.value: In VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs or the terminal.

data.name: ForCopilotDoesWell
data.value: Copilot works in the editors many teams already use: VS Code, Visual Studio, JetBrains IDEs, Xcode, Eclipse and more.

data.value: Type / in Copilot Chat and pick the skill, or just ask: Copilot loads one when your request fits it.

data.value: Open it in VS Code

data.value: From $0 a month

data.name: ForCopilotCostText
data.value: Copilot Free to start; Pro is $10 a month.

data.name: ForCopilotQuestionPlan
data.value: Do I need a paid Copilot plan?

data.name: ForCopilotAnswerPlan
data.value: No. Copilot Free works, and a model you add with your own key works even without a Copilot plan. Pro is $10 a month.

data.name: ForCopilotQuestionModels
data.value: Can Copilot use DeepSeek, Qwen or a model on my computer?

data.name: ForCopilotAnswerModels
data.value: Yes. Add it in VS Code with your own key: Manage Language Models, then Add Models. The provider bills you, and it doesn't count against Copilot's limits.

data.value: One app, as bit Fabric makes it with one command: its website, its Android, iOS, Windows and macOS apps and its server, with every environment and every customer it serves. A second product is a second project.

data.name: Cost

data.name: CostPageTitle
data.value: Why a real app costs less with bit Fabric

data.name: CostPageDescription
data.value: Judge the cost of your project, not what a single token costs: how many tokens a task takes, in Anthropic's own figures, and how many a whole project takes, where bit Fabric has already built much of it and cuts the rounds of rework.

data.value: Judge the cost of your project, not the price of a token.

data.value: A token's price is the first number you see. What you really pay depends on how many tokens each task takes, and how many tasks your whole project takes. That is where bit Fabric makes the difference.

data.name: CliRefNew
data.value: Creates a project and gets it ready to run: the tools it needs, the build, git, its database and your editor.

data.name: CliRefSetup
data.value: Gets a project that exists ready on this computer, cloning it first when given its repository's address. It also adds an app later, such as Android.

data.name: CliRefRun
data.value: Builds and starts the project: the website and its server, or the Android, iOS, macOS or Windows app.

data.name: CliRefCodespace
data.value: Runs the project on GitHub Codespaces, in its branch's codespace, which it reuses and creates only when there's none, with the app's addresses working on this computer.

data.name: CliRefDiff
data.value: Shows what changed in the project's starting point between two versions, as one commit your AI brings into your project.

data.name: CliRefDoctor
data.value: Checks this computer for the tools a project needs, and installs what's missing with --fix.

data.name: CliRefTrust
data.value: Marks a project's folder as trusted for VS Code, Claude Code, Copilot CLI, Codex and Gemini CLI.

data.name: CliRefClean
data.value: Deletes the project's build outputs and downloaded packages, so the next build starts fresh.

data.name: CliRefRename
data.value: Renames the project everywhere its name appears: files, folders, code, the database and the app's id.

data.name: CliRefRemove
data.value: Deletes a folder for good in 10 seconds at most, stopping the apps that keep its files in use.

data.name: CliRefMigration
data.value: Adds and removes the database's migrations, and bundles them for the database on your server.

data.name: CliRefApi
data.value: Checks that the server's api still works for the app versions your users run, and keeps each release's api.

data.name: CliRefTranslate
data.value: Fills in the missing translations of the app's texts with an AI model, and checks that none is missing.

data.name: CliRefDecode
data.value: Reads an error report of a minified app back into the names its code has.

data.name: CliRefKeys
data.value: Creates the keys and certificates the project signs and encrypts with: web push, the server's certificate, and the Android and iOS apps' signing.

data.name: CliRefPipeline
data.value: Fills in the secrets the GitHub Actions workflows use, and locks the repository down.

data.name: CliRefAotProfile
data.value: Writes the profile that makes the web app fast while its download stays small.

data.name: CliRefTelemetry
data.value: Shows what bit CLI reports to the bit platform team, and changes it.

data.name: CliRefUpdate
data.value: Updates bit CLI to the newest version. bit new and a project's commands do it by themselves.

data.name: CliRefLicense
data.value: Shows the project's license, and the link that gets it one, free.

data.name: CliRefAbout
data.value: Shows where this build of bit CLI comes from, and how to verify it.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckTitle
data.value: Fact-check us in under a minute

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckLead
data.value: Don't take our word for it. Let the AI you already use and trust every day give you a first verdict: it checks our claims against the articles they cite and the source code, and tells you whether bit Fabric fits your business.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckShowHow
data.value: Show me how

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckHide
data.value: Hide

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckYourAITitle
data.value: Have Claude Desktop, Codex or another AI?

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckYourAIText
data.value: Hand it this site: every claim here links to its source, an article or the source code. Copy this into your AI, fill in your business or pick one above, and it fact-checks bit Fabric and tells you, from your own business and needs, whether it really fits.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckYourselfTitle
data.value: Or see for yourself

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckYourselfText
data.value: Read the site yourself, or ask our assistant: chat with it, or even call it. It reads every page and the source code, and this chat stays on your device: our servers don't keep it.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckAskAssistant
data.value: Ask our assistant

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckChatPrompt
data.value: Is bit Fabric worth starting with for my business? Ask me what you need to know, then fact-check it for me.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckPrompt
data.value:
Fact-check bit Fabric ({0}) for me, as a skeptical reviewer, not a salesperson. My business: [what it does and how big it is] What my app must do: [what it must do, on which devices, and what matters most]
Connect to the MCP server {1} and call its EvaluateBitFabric tool with the two above. If you can't connect to it, send its JSON-RPC requests (tools/list, then tools/call) to that address yourself; if you can't do that either, read {0}/llms-full.txt. Then check the claims that matter to me yourself: each links to its source, an article or the code at https://github.com/bitfoundation/bitfabric. Tell me in under 200 words what holds and what doesn't, what it would cost me in time, money and skills, and whether it's worth starting with: yes, no or not yet, and why.

data.name: AppHomeFactCheckExamples
data.value: Start from a common business, or fill in your own:
